title: Infected von Meyenburg complex causing recurrent gram‑negative septicaemia: the critical diagnostic role of FDG‑PET/CT in a patient with hidradenitis suppurativa.
abstract: Background von Meyenburg complex (VMC) is a rare ductal plate malformation, typically presenting as asymptomatic benign intrahepatic biliary microhamartomas. However, when secondarily infected, VMC can become the source of cryptic recurrent septicaemia, posing a substantial diagnostic challenge, particularly in patients with a known history of chronic source of comorbid infection. Case presentation A 73-year-old man with long-standing hidradenitis suppurativa presented with over ten episodes of recurrent gram-negative septicaemia. Extensive conventional imaging, including a 67 Gallium scintigraphy in another hospital, failed to identify an infectious source. Due to persistent diagnostic uncertainty, ¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT was performed. The scan revealed an enlarged liver with heterogeneously increased ¹⁸F-FDG uptake exhibiting an "inverted pyramidal" metabolic configuration: a wide base of activity along the subcapsular dome of superior hepatic segments converged centripetally towards the porta hepatis, thereby casting a tree-like three-dimensional anatomy of the biliary radicles. CT findings were non-specific, showing vaguely scattered mixed densities, greatly outnumbered by the hypermetabolic foci. Constellation of these findings suggests a non-dilated ductal infectious process, leading to the presumptive diagnosis of infected VMC with micro-abscesses. Subsequent MRI/MRCP confirmed numerous tiny T2‑weighted bright signals of varying sizes and intensities in agreement with the "starry sky" pattern of biliary hamartomas. Targeted levofloxacin therapy based on susceptibility testing resulted in resolution of fever and septic parameters. A follow-up ¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT scan three weeks after treatment demonstrated complete metabolic quiescence and resolution of previously documented intrahepatic hypermetabolic foci. Conclusion ¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT has proven value in investigation for fever of unknown origin. This case illustrates the value of this imaging not only in precise localization of the infectious source but also provides a suggestive metabolic pattern leading to the diagnosis of a rare congenital biliary condition, VMC, as a hidden source of infection otherwise masked by other comorbid infectious foci. Revealing the true source of loculated infection and its mechanism of spread leads to appropriate antibiotic therapy and treatment monitoring.

title: Detection rate of PSMA PET MRI (18 F-Flotufolastat) at the onset of biochemical recurrence following radical prostatectomy.
abstract: Purpose The optimal timing to obtain the initial PET-PSMA imaging study when disease recurrence is suspected following RP is controversial. Methods 24 subjects with new onset of BCR following RP were enrolled. The initial PET MRI (study #1) was performed within 2 months of signing informed consent. Salvage treatment was offered only if site(s) of disease recurrence were identified by study #1. A second PSMA PET MRI (study #2) was performed 1 year following Study 1, or sooner if the 6-month PSA was > 0.5 ng/ml. PET/MR was performed in a dedicated scanner which allows simultaneous acquisition of PET and MR images following the IV administration of 8 m Ci of 18 F-Flotufolastat (18F-rH PSMA, Blue Earth Diagnostics, UK). Results Disease recurrence was identified in 25% and 40% of subjects by study #1 and study #2, respectively. PSA doubling time with and without disease recurrence on study #2 was 12.8 months (IQR 4.0-17.2) and 20.8 months (20.8 months (IQR 9.1-51.7), respectively (p = 0.27). PSA prior to RP but not age, pathological grade, stage margin status or time to recurrence were significantly different between subjects with and without localization of disease recurrence. Conclusions The 25% disease detection and localizations justify performing PSMA PET MRI imaging at the onset of BCR. If the initial PSMA PET MRI does not identify site(s) of disease, our study supports repeating a PSMA PET study when the PSA is > 0.5 ng/ml or if the PSA doubling time is < 1 year. Clinical trial record The study is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov with study number NCT05678322.- Registration date 12/28/2022 URL of trial registry record: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05678322.

title: Expanding role of nuclear medicine in cardiac amyloidosis: insights from the EJNMMI collection.
abstract: Recent advances in nuclear medicine are reshaping the evaluation of cardiac amyloidosis, as highlighted by the recent collection published in EJNMMI (collection link: https://link.springer.com/collections/igfdhcddjg). This commentary summarizes key insights from these studies, emphasizing the evolving shift from conventional diagnostic imaging toward a more integrated and comprehensive approach. Emerging developments include novel amyloid PET tracers, improved diagnostic accuracy with SPECT/CT, multimodality imaging strategies, and enhanced assessment of systemic disease burden extending beyond the left ventricle. There is also growing interest in longitudinal monitoring, pre-symptomatic detection, and the role of artificial intelligence. Together, these advances position nuclear medicine as an essential tool for disease characterization, risk stratification, and treatment assessment.

title: Effect of data-driven gating on the quantification of prostate cancer metastases in <sup>68</sup>Ga-PSMA- and ¹⁸F-DCFPyL-PSMA PET/CT.
abstract: Background PSMA PET/CT using 18 F‑DCFPyL and 68 Ga‑labelled tracers is central to prostate cancer staging, but 68 Ga‑PSMA may show reduced sensitivity and quantitative accuracy, partly due to respiratory motion and lower spatial resolution. Device-based motion‑correction methods have limitations. Data‑driven gating (DDG) offers a hardware‑free alternative, though its impact on PSMA PET, especially 68 Ga‑PSMA has not been systematically evaluated. To evaluate the quantitative and qualitative performance of the DDG motion-correction method in 68 Ga-PSMA and 18 F-DCFPyL-PSMA PET/CT, focusing on metastatic lymph node, lung, and bone lesions, and to assess its robustness across tracers. Methods This retrospective study included patients with biopsy‑proven prostate cancer who underwent 68 Ga‑PSMA or 18 F‑DCFPyL PSMA PET/CT for primary staging or biochemical recurrence and had metastatic disease. Motion correction was applied using the OncoFreeze AI™ data‑driven gating (OFAI‑DDG) method. Metastatic lesions were segmented semi‑automatically, and SUV metrics, image noise, and contrast‑to‑noise ratio were quantified by anatomical site in both OFAI-DDG and static images. Qualitative image quality was independently scored by two experienced readers. Statistical analyses included non‑parametric tests, Bland-Altman agreement, regression analyses, tracer comparison, and inter‑reader reliability assessment. Results After exclusions, 23 68 Ga‑PSMA and 40 18 F‑PSMA patients were analyzed, yielding 133 and 192 metastatic lesions, respectively. OFAI‑DDG reconstruction significantly increased SUV mean and SUV max compared with static imaging for both tracers across bone, lymph node, and lung lesions (p < 0.0001), with the largest gains in lung lesions. CNR improved for most lesion types, and image noise was significantly reduced. Qualitative analysis showed better image quality, sharpness, and noise with OFAI‑DDG, with high inter‑reader agreement. OFAI‑DDG performance was robust across tracers and largely independent of lesion location. Conclusions This study demonstrates that OFAI‑DDG significantly improves PSMA PET/CT image quality and quantitative accuracy compared with standard static imaging. The improvements were observed for both 68 Ga‑PSMA and 18 F‑PSMA tracers, indicating tracer‑independent robustness. The OFAI‑DDG simplified the workflow and reduced time used for patient set-up, while enhancing lesion visualization and quantitative reliability without altering lesion detection, supporting its clinical value for metastatic prostate cancer imaging.

title: Post-embolization dynamic changes in Obsidio Conformable Embolic: volume and radiodensity analysis.
abstract: To characterize the temporal dynamic and clinical remodeling of the Obsidio™ Conformable Embolic (Obsidio) post endovascular delivery using longitudinal quantitative CT volumetry and Hounsfield unit (HU) attenuation. This retrospective, single-center cohort study included 21 patients (30 vessels) embolized with Obsidio for acute hemorrhage or hypervascular tumor between 2023 and 2026. Patients had at least two follow-up computed tomography (CT) scans. The primary endpoint was the percent change in embolic cast volume and HU attenuation, measured using standardized Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS) segmentation tools. Secondary endpoints included assessment for recanalization. All embolizations were technically successful (100%). On the first follow-up CT (median 12 days), the mean Obsidio volume was 89.33 ± 13.86% of the original volume (p = 0.0002). On the second follow-up (median 36 days), the volume was 79.51 ± 19.76% of baseline volume (p = 0.0004), representing 20.49% reduction. On third follow-up CT (median 76 days), volume was 85.2 ± 18.92% (p = 0.047). On the fourth follow-up CT, volume was 66.76 ± 16.9% (p = 0.0048). On the fifth follow-up CT, volume was 60.15 ± 3.15% (p = 0.00001) The average volume reduction rate decelerated from 0.99%/day to 0.71%/day to 0.17%/day then stabilized at 0.2%/day. Concurrently, mean Hounsfield unit attenuation increased by 4.85% (p = 0.06) on the second follow-up CT scan. No evidence of recanalization, distal embolization, or cast fragmentation was observed on any of CT scans. The Obsidio embolic cast undergoes progressive reduction in volume and increase in HU attenuation over time without evidence of vessel recanalization. This temporal dynamic of Obsidio embolic is consistent with bioresorption of its gelatin and water components, supporting the concept of persistent occlusion via in vivo remodeling.

title: Stroke-associated pneumonia: from immunodepression to bedside management and future research directions.
abstract: Stroke-associated pneumonia (SAP) is one of the most frequent complications after acute stroke, affecting approximately one in eight stroke patients. Besides prolonged hospitalisation and increased healthcare costs, it is also a major risk factor for mortality and poor functional recovery. The pathophysiology of SAP is driven by two converging processes: impaired local airway defence due to dysphagia as well as reduced airway clearance reflexes, and systemic stroke-induced immunodepression driven by dysfunction of the autonomic nervous system. While post-stroke immunodepression is a major risk factor for SAP, it might limit unwanted autoimmune responses within the brain. Conversely, SAP itself may drive neuroinflammation and contribute to post-stroke cognitive impairment. Despite its clinical importance, high-quality evidence to guide practice on prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of SAP remains scarce and guideline recommendations are mostly based on expert consensus. Diagnosis of SAP is suggested to be based on standardised clinical criteria supported by chest radiography and C-reactive protein as an adjunct where uncertainty persists. After diagnosis, guidelines suggest prompt empirical antibiotic therapy according to local protocols. In contrast, preventive antibiotics, even for high-risk patients, neither improve clinical outcome nor reduce SAP frequency. Currently recommended preventive strategies for SAP therefore mostly focus on dysphagia management and early mobilisation. This review integrates the pathophysiology, long-term consequences of SAP and further research directions based on the current knowledge on post-stroke immunology with prevention, diagnosis and treatment of SAP as set out in the recent European Stroke Organisation guideline and related guidelines.

title: A web modular AI interface for brain tumor MRI classification using deep learning models.
abstract: In order to improve patient outcomes and treatment processes, early and precise diagnosis of brain tumors is crucial. Despite the strong performance shown by deep learning models in classifying brain tumors from MRI scans, integrating these models into user-friendly clinical workflows remains challenging. This study presents a web-based AI platform designed for brain tumor classification using MRI images. The platform enables users to upload MRI scans, apply standardized preprocessing, select between different deep learning models, and receive real-time predictions. A custom convolutional neural network (CNN), pretrained VGG19, and pretrained Xception were evaluated using a publicly available T1-weighted contrast-enhanced brain MRI dataset of approximately 7,000 images across four classes: glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor. The dataset lacks patient demographic and clinical metadata, limiting assessment of clinical generalizability. The models achieved test accuracies of 96.03%, 98%, and 96%, respectively, with VGG19 demonstrating the best performance. The study is limited by the use of a single public, slice-based dataset and the absence of external clinical validation; future work will focus on multi-sequence MRI and independent clinical cohorts.

title: Adapting Segment Anything Model 3 for concept-driven lesion segmentation in medical images: an experimental study.
abstract: Accurate segmentation of lesions is fundamental for medical image analysis. However, most existing approaches are designed for specific anatomical sites and imaging modalities, limiting their applicability in heterogeneous clinical environments. Recent vision-language foundation models have enabled concept-driven segmentation of natural images, offering a promising path toward more flexible and generalizable medical image segmentation. However, to the best of the authors' knowledge, concept-prompt-based lesion segmentation in medical images, particularly using the latest Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3), has not been thoroughly examined. In this paper, the authors present a systematic investigation of the SAM3 framework for lesion segmentation. An extensive evaluation of SAM3 was first conducted using geometric bounding boxes and concept-based text and image exemplars as prompts for lesion segmentation across multiple cancer types and imaging modalities, including magnetic resonance imaging, computed tomography, ultrasound, dermoscopy, and endoscopic imaging, with particular emphasis on volumetric medical imaging datasets. To improve robustness and segmentation accuracy, additional knowledge into the input representation was further integrated, including predictions from adjacent slices, multiparametric imaging information, and prior annotations. In addition, the study compared different SAM3 fine-tuning strategies on the BraTS2023-MET dataset, including partial module fine-tuning, adapter-based optimization, and full-model fine-tuning, under different training objectives. Extensive experiments conducted on 13 datasets covering 11 lesion types demonstrate that SAM3 achieves strong cross-modality generalization and accurate instance-specific lesion delineation. These results highlight the potential of concept-driven foundation models for scalable and practical medical-image segmentation in real-world clinical settings. The source code and dataset splits are publicly available at https://github.com/apple1986/lesion-sam3 .

title: Swin-WaveNet: frequency-guided boundary restoration for robust skin lesion segmentation.
abstract: Accurate skin lesion segmentation remains difficult when dermoscopic boundaries are fragmented by hair occlusion, uneven illumination, or weak local contrast. To address this problem, the authors propose Swin-WaveNet, a frequency-guided encoder-decoder that combines a Swin Transformer backbone with wavelet decomposition and selective state-space modeling. Rather than passing skip features directly to the decoder, the proposed method separates low-frequency semantic information from high-frequency details, selectively refines boundary-related responses, and suppresses artifact-induced activation prior to feature reconstruction. The main results are reported as the mean and standard deviation of the sample over three runs. Swin-WaveNet achieved a Dice score of 89.69% ± 0.51% and a 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) of [Formula: see text] pixels on the International Skin Imaging Collaboration (ISIC) 2018 dataset. Without fine-tuning on ISIC 2017, it obtained a Dice score of 91.69% ± 1.36% and an HD95 of [Formula: see text] pixels. On Kvasir-SEG, the model achieved a Dice score of 91.63% ± 0.57% and an HD95 of [Formula: see text] pixels. In a single-run component ablation, the complete model improved the Dice score by 0.96 percentage points and reduced HD95 by 1.16 pixels relative to the internal baseline. These results indicate that frequency-selective feature processing can help preserve weak or interrupted lesion boundaries.

title: Utilizing bedside VExUS and the S-prime velocity for real-time assessment of venous congestion on right ventricular function in heart failure.
abstract: Background Right ventricular (RV) function is a major determinant of outcomes in heart failure (HF), yet RV systolic performance and venous congestion (VC) are often evaluated separately. We investigated the relationship between tricuspid annular systolic velocity (S'), a tissue Doppler marker of RV systolic function and systemic VC measured by the Venous Excess Ultrasound (VExUS) score in patients with HF. In addition, RV-pulmonary artery (RV-PA) coupling parameters including TAPSE/PASP and S'/PASP were evaluated across VExUS grades. Methods In this prospective, single-center observational study, 155 patients admitted with decompensated HF underwent standardized echocardiography, including VExUS assessment and S' measurement. Lung Ultrasound Score (LUS), RV-PA coupling indices, clinical characteristics, in-hospital mortality, and acute kidney injury (AKI) were also recorded. Results The mean age was 57.5 years, with 68% of the cohort being males. A significant inverse correlation was observed between VExUS grade and S' velocity (p < 0.001). Patients with VExUS Grade 0 had higher S' velocities (median = 11.0 cm/s), while those with Grade 3 had the lowest (8.5 cm/s). Increasing VExUS grades were also associated with progressive worsening of TAPSE, TAPSE/PASP, and S'/PASP ratios, suggesting impaired RV-PA coupling with increasing venous congestion. Both higher VExUS grades and reduced S' were associated with more severe pulmonary congestion on LUS (p < 0.001 and p = 0.003, respectively). Although patients with higher VExUS grades and lower S' values trended towards worse outcomes, neither parameter significantly predicted in-hospital mortality or AKI. Conclusion Systemic VC and RV systolic function are strongly and inversely related in HF. The combined use of VExUS and S' provides an integrated bedside assessment of hemodynamic status that may help guide decongestive therapy. Integration of RV-PA coupling parameters may further enhance bedside evaluation of hemodynamic compromise in HF patients. Additionally, S'/PASP and TAPSE/PASP demonstrated comparable trends across all HF groups, suggesting that S'/PASP may serve as a practical alternative marker of RV-PA coupling in heart failure patients. Larger studies are needed to determine their prognostic utility for predicting mortality and organ injury. Trial registration This trial was registered with Clinical Trial Registry-India ( https://www.ctri.nic.in/ ), Trial Number - CTRI/2024/10/075219 on 14/10/2024.

title: Robot-assisted thoracoscopic resection of a costal cartilage chondrosarcoma mimicking anterior mediastinal teratoma: a case report.
abstract: Background Chondrosarcoma arising from the costal cartilage is extremely rare. When such a tumor extends toward the mediastinum, it may present as a well-defined mass that is difficult to distinguish from a primary anterior mediastinal tumor. We report a case diagnosed preoperatively as a mature teratoma but later proven to be a grade 1 chondrosarcoma of the costal cartilage. Case presentation A 66-year-old asymptomatic woman was incidentally found to have an abnormal shadow on chest imaging. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed a well-defined, calcified mass measuring 37 × 31 × 21 mm in the anterior mediastinum, adjacent to the left costal arch; bone-window and reformatted images did not clearly demonstrate continuity with the adjacent costal cartilage. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated T1-weighted hyperintensity with signal loss on fat-suppressed imaging, consistent with a fatty component, and no invasion of surrounding structures. Positron emission tomography-computed tomography showed low fluorodeoxyglucose uptake and no distant metastasis, and tumor markers were normal. A preoperative diagnosis of mature teratoma was made, and resection was planned. Robot-assisted thoracoscopic surgery was performed via a three-port right-sided approach. Intraoperatively, the tumor lay in the narrow space between the heart and the sternum, with direct continuity with the left sixth costal cartilage suggesting its origin; the tumor-cartilage boundary could not be identified, and the cartilage was divided at the tumor interface. The postoperative course was uneventful. Pathological examination revealed chondrocyte-like tumor cells with mild nuclear atypia, consistent with a grade 1 chondrosarcoma of the costal cartilage; residual tumor could not be excluded (Rx). A multidisciplinary tumor board elected surveillance, and no recurrence has been observed at 18 months postoperatively. Conclusions Costal cartilage chondrosarcoma belongs in the differential diagnosis of a calcified anterior mediastinal mass because preoperative recognition determines whether a wide or marginal resection is planned, and a minimally invasive approach must not compromise the surgical margin when malignancy is suspected. The right-sided robot-assisted thoracoscopic approach provided favorable visualization and maneuverability in this confined retrosternal location, but its oncological safety cannot be generalized from a single case.

title: Primary pulmonary hyalinizing clear cell carcinoma harboring EWSR1::ATF1 fusion: a case report.
abstract: Background Hyalinizing clear cell carcinoma (HCCC) is a rare salivary gland-type tumor that occasionally arises in the lung. As it shows substantial morphological overlap with mucoepidermoid carcinoma (MEC), definitive diagnosis can be challenging. Therefore, molecular testing is essential, as MEC typically harbors CRTC1/3::MAML2 fusions, whereas HCCC is characterized by EWSR1 fusions. Case presentation A 60-year-old woman presented with persistent cough and hemoptysis. Imaging revealed a 3.0-cm solid nodule in the left lower lobe adjacent to the bronchus. She underwent robot-assisted left lower lobectomy with lymph node dissection. Histologically, the tumor consisted of uniform epithelioid cells with clear-to-pale eosinophilic cytoplasm arranged in nests and cords within prominent hyalinized stroma. Cytologic atypia was minimal. Immunohistochemically, tumor cells were positive for CK7, CK5/6, and p40 and negative for TTF-1. Venous invasion was present without lymph node metastasis. Break-apart fluorescence in situ hybridization revealed rearrangements of EWSR1 and ATF1, strongly supporting the presence of an EWSR1::ATF1 fusion, whereas MAML2 rearrangement was absent. The patient remains recurrence-free 1 year after surgery. Conclusion Accurately distinguishing primary pulmonary HCCC, which is rare and may mimic MEC, is essential for appropriate pathological classification and prognostic assessment. It is also important for thoracic surgeons to consider HCCC during the differential diagnosis of centrally located or endobronchial pulmonary tumors, particularly when a definitive preoperative diagnosis is challenging. Integrating histopathology with molecular testing for EWSR1 and MAML2 rearrangements is critical for accurate diagnosis.

title: Müllerian-type high-grade serous carcinoma presenting exclusively with pleural lesions and no detectable abdominopelvic primary tumor: a case report.
abstract: Background Müllerian-type high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC) most commonly originates from the fallopian tube, ovary, or peritoneum and usually presents with abdominopelvic disease. Thoracic presentation without a detectable abdominopelvic primary tumor is extremely rare and poses a diagnostic challenge. Case presentation We report the case of a 60-year-old woman who was referred to our hospital after pleural thickening was detected during a routine medical checkup. Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed left pleural thickening with mild pleural effusion. Thoracoscopic pleural biopsy was performed. Histopathological examination demonstrated spindle-shaped cells with mild nuclear atypia, with scattered calcifications and osteocyte-like elements. Immunohistochemical staining showed positivity for PAX8, WT-1, AE1/AE3, CK7, p16, and p53, and negativity for calretinin, D2-40, TTF-1, and Napsin A, supporting a Müllerian-type HGSC. Diagnostic/staging laparoscopy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy revealed no macroscopic tumor or disseminated lesions. Both ovaries and fallopian tubes were carefully examined pathologically, with the fallopian tubes examined using the SEE-FIM protocol. No malignant lesion or serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC) was identified. Peritoneal washing cytology was negative. p53 and Ki-67 immunohistochemistry of the tubo-ovarian specimens was not performed. Discussion The absence of a detectable abdominopelvic primary tumor after radiological, laparoscopic, and pathological evaluation suggests an extremely rare thoracic presentation of Müllerian-type HGSC. Both ovaries and fallopian tubes were carefully examined pathologically, including examination of the fallopian tubes using the SEE-FIM protocol, and no malignant lesion or STIC was identified. Nevertheless, an occult microscopic Müllerian primary cannot be completely excluded, particularly because p53 and Ki-67 immunohistochemistry of the tubo-ovarian specimens was not performed. Primary pleural Müllerian carcinoma, EOPPC, and Müllerian-type HGSC of undetermined primary origin therefore remain possible classifications. Müllerian-type HGSC should be considered in the differential diagnosis of pleural tumors in women, even when no abdominopelvic primary tumor is identified. Comprehensive radiological, laparoscopic, and pathological evaluation is important for determining the most appropriate classification. In the absence of an identified primary site, classification should remain cautious, and EOPPC should be regarded as a possible interpretation rather than a definitive diagnosis.

title: Massive enlargement of a previously unrecognized bronchogenic cyst over 8 years with intracystic hemorrhage and complex surgical resection: a case report.
abstract: Background Bronchogenic cysts are usually asymptomatic and are often detected incidentally; however, they may become symptomatic due to infection, hemorrhage, or enlargement. We report a case of a previously unrecognized bronchogenic cyst that showed substantial enlargement from 4.8 to 13 cm over an 8-year interval, with intracystic hemorrhage, ultimately requiring partial resection of the esophageal muscularis. Case presentation A man in his 20s presented with upper abdominal pain and nausea. Computed tomography revealed a 13-cm mass extending from below the tracheal bifurcation to the level of the gastric cardia. A CT scan obtained eight years earlier during the evaluation of abdominal pain had shown a 4.8-cm cystic lesion below the tracheal bifurcation, demonstrating substantial enlargement over the intervening period. Although conservative treatment was attempted, compressive symptoms persisted; therefore, surgical resection was performed for definitive diagnosis and symptom relief. Severe inflammatory adhesions necessitated right open thoracotomy with partial resection of the esophageal muscularis. The cyst contained a large hematoma, and histopathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of a bronchogenic cyst with intracystic hemorrhage. title: Toward Clinically Actionable Prediction of Recurrence and Metastatic Progression in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Purpose Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has high rates of early recurrence (ER), occult metastasis, and poor survival despite curative-intent therapy. Predictive factors and models span clinical, biomarker, imaging, radiomics, pathologic, and molecular domains, but clinical readiness remains uncertain. Methods We performed a systematic review in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses. Five databases were searched for studies evaluating predictors or models of PDAC recurrence, metastasis, lymph node metastasis (LNM), occult metastatic disease, disease-free survival (DFS) or recurrence-free survival, or recurrence patterns. Studies were screened and coded for end point, modality, model type, validation, discrimination, calibration, clinical utility, and predictor timing. Results Of 234 full-text records, 208 studies were included, comprising 144 prediction models and 64 predictor/prognostic factor studies. Computed tomography/radiomics (141/208), clinical/electronic health record variables (104/208), and serum/urine biomarkers (46/208) were the most common modalities. External validation, calibration, and decision-curve analyses were reported in 52, 36, and 38 model studies, respectively. AUCs ranged from 0.70 to 0.92 for ER, 0.75-0.95 for LNM, and 0.71-0.88 for liver or occult metastasis; DFS/relapse-free survival models had C-indices of 0.62-0.82. One externally validated occult-metastasis model had a C-statistic of 0.56. Model maturity was limited by retrospective design, heterogeneous end points, incomplete calibration reporting, and postoperative variables in preoperative models. Conclusion Prediction models for PDAC recurrence and metastatic progression are rapidly expanding, particularly through radiomics, machine learning, and multimodal modeling. Clinical translation requires decision-aligned design, transparent reporting, external validation, calibration, interpretability, and prospective evaluation of clinical utility.

title: Feasibility of Lung Cancer Computed Tomography Screening in Jordan: Resource Assessment and Health Impact Modeling.
abstract: Purpose Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer mortality in Jordan, with most cases presenting at advanced stages. Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) screening has demonstrated mortality reduction in high-risk populations in developed countries. This study evaluates the feasibility and potential impact of implementing LDCT lung cancer screening in Jordan and includes a health benefit analysis. Materials and methods We analyzed Jordan's at-risk population using NELSON trial eligibility criteria and 2019 STEPS smoking survey data. Current radiological resources were assessed through official government sources and compared with international benchmarks from countries with established lung cancer screening programs. Health benefits were modeled using stage migration data from the NELSON trial applied to Jordan's lung cancer registry data (2013-2022) to calculate a benefit analysis. Results An estimated 622,499 Jordanians, age 50-74 years, meet screening eligibility criteria. Jordan has 37.69 radiologists per million population (PMP; range, 6.03-62.47 across governorates), compared with the modeled minimum of 65.63. CT scanner availability is 16.37 PMP, very close to the minimum requirement of 16.76 but with significant geographic disparities. Modeling suggests screening could increase stage I diagnoses from 8.38% to 35.28% and reduce stage IV diagnoses from 73% to 54%, projecting a reduction of 34.93 advanced-stage presentations annually. Conclusion Although Jordan approaches adequacy in CT scanner availability, significant radiologist shortages and geographic disparities present major implementation challenges for LDCT lung cancer screening. Modeling uncertainties and infrastructure gaps necessitates pilot studies to validate assumptions before national implementation. Targeted infrastructure investment and workforce development are essential prerequisites for effective lung cancer screening in Jordan.

title: Leveraging Digital Histopathology to Build Capacity and Collaboration Toward the Diagnosis of Pediatric Solid Tumors in Mexico.
abstract: Purpose Pediatric pathology in Mexico remains limited by an uneven distribution of specialized training and constrained resources, which can affect the accuracy of pediatric malignancy diagnosis. This study aimed to evaluate national diagnostic capacity for common organ-based pediatric solid tumors-renal tumors, neuroblastic tumors, and hepatic neoplasms-through a retrospective hybrid central pathology review. A secondary objective was to identify targeted areas for capacity building and strengthen collaborative networking. Materials and methods A hybrid retrospective pathology review (2005-2023) was conducted across eight institutions that treat pediatric oncology patients. Eligible cases included off-therapy patients age 0-18 years diagnosed with renal, hepatic, or neuroblastic tumors. Paraffin blocks, slides, clinical data, and original pathology reports were submitted. Cases underwent conventional pathology review, digital slide scanning, and joint virtual evaluation. Final diagnoses were compared between original, conventional central pathology review, and digital review, and individualized feedback was provided to each institution. Results A total of 162 specimens were reviewed, including 584 original stained slides, 940 paraffin blocks, and 1,168 digitized slides. At least 54 online review sessions were conducted, and 24 virtual feedback sessions were held. Overall diagnostic concordance across original, central, and digital evaluations was 80% for renal tumors, 90.9% for neuroblastic tumors, and 92.1% for hepatic neoplasms. Common limitations included inconsistent/inadequate sampling and incomplete/erroneous subclassification and reporting. Conclusion Findings confirm strong baseline diagnostic capabilities for common pediatric solid tumors across participating Mexican centers, while highlighting specific gaps in sampling, reporting standardization, and access to ancillary testing. The project facilitated the creation of a pediatric pathology network, demonstrating that a hybrid centralized-digital review model can strengthen specialized pediatric pathology capacity in resource-limited settings.

title: Dose-Escalated Focal Salvage High-Dose-Rate Brachytherapy and Genomic Classifier Risk Stratification in Radiorecurrent Prostate Cancer: The F-SHARP Phase I/II Clinical Trial.
abstract: Purpose Prospective data on the management of intraprostatic radiorecurrence (IPR) after definitive radiotherapy (RT) and use of genomic classifiers (GC) in this setting are limited. We hypothesized that dose-escalated focal salvage high-dose-rate brachytherapy (DE-fsHDR) would be safe and effective, and that GC would risk stratify patients who may benefit from treatment intensification. Methods F-SHARP is a multi-institutional phase I/II trial of DE-fsHDR for IPR after any form of RT for localized prostate cancer. Patients received up to 30 Gy in 1-2 fractions. The primary objective was to determine the acute RT-related grade ≥3 CTCAE v4.03 genitourinary and GI toxicity rates. Secondary end points included all-grade toxicity, quality of life (QoL; EPIC-26 and International Prostate Symptom Score), disease control, and survival. GC analysis used a clinical-grade transcriptome assay (Veracyte, San Diego, CA). Time-to-event outcomes included biochemical progression-free survival (bPFS), radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS), local recurrence-free survival (LRFS), and metastasis-free survival (MFS). Results Twenty-four participants received one fraction and 38 received two fractions (N = 62). The median follow-up was 39.4 months. No acute grade 3 toxicities occurred. Two patients (3.2%) had late grade 3 toxicity. QoL changes did not meet criteria for a minimal clinically important difference. Three-year survival rates were 62.7% (bPFS), 67.5% (rPFS), 73.0% (LRFS), and 85.9% (MFS); there were no differences between fractionation groups (all P > .05). Among 31 patients with GC results, higher scores were associated with worse bPFS, rPFS, LRFS, and MFS. All patients with GC score >0.85 (n = 4) experienced biochemical, local, and metastatic recurrence. Conclusion DE-fsHDR is a safe and effective salvage treatment for IPR. GC score is a promising prognostic tool in patients undergoing salvage local therapy for IPR and warrants further study to guide treatment intensification.

title: Decoding Treatment Response and Prognosis in Unresectable Locally Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer by Integrating Spatiotemporal Heterogeneity From 18 F-FDG Positron Emission Tomography-Computed Tomography: A Multicenter Study.
abstract: Purpose Treatment response in unresectable locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer (LA-NSCLC) is highly variable due to marked intratumoral heterogeneity, while existing predictive biomarkers lack accuracy. We aimed to develop and validate a pretreatment 18 F-FDG positron emission tomography (PET)-computed tomography (CT)-derived spatiotemporal heterogeneity model to predict treatment response and prognosis in unresectable LA-NSCLC, and to explore its biological underpinnings. Materials and methods In a multicenter cohort of 434 patients with unresectable LA-NSCLC (training: n = 215; internal validation: n = 93; external validation: n = 126), treatment response was classified as responsive or nonresponsive based on initial assessment. Four distinct habitats (PEThigh-CThigh, PETlow-CTlow, PETlow-CThigh, and PEThigh-CTlow) were generated via the Otsu algorithm. Temporal heterogeneity was quantified using metabolic hotspot displacement (normalized distance from the hotspot to the tumor centroid and normalized distance from the hotspot to the tumor periphery) and integrated with spatial radiomics to build a multidimensional spatiotemporal model. Model performance was evaluated against conventional metrics, with interpretability enhanced via nomogram and SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis. Survival outcomes were assessed using Kaplan-Meier curves, and public transcriptomic data were analyzed to characterize underlying pathways. Results The spatiotemporal model accurately predicted treatment response with AUCs of 0.822 (training), 0.821 (internal validation), and 0.810 (external validation), significantly outperforming conventional whole-tumor PET-CT models. It maintained robust generalizability across treatment subgroups and effectively stratified patients by progression-free survival and overall survival ( P < .01). PEThigh-CThigh habitat volume fraction correlated with treatment resistance, whereas PETlow-CTlow habitat correlated with better response. Exploratory pathway analysis highlighted key pathways involving drug metabolism, glycolytic reprogramming, and immune microenvironment remodeling. Conclusion This study establishes a noninvasive spatiotemporal heterogeneity biomarker based on 18 F-FDG PET-CT that reliably predicts treatment response and prognostic outcomes in unresectable LA-NSCLC. It offers valuable insights for personalized clinical decision making and supports precision oncology.

title: Concurrent thyroid and abdominal diffuse large B-cell lymphoma arising in the milieu of chronic fibrosing thyroiditis.
abstract: Firm tender thyroid masses present a diagnostic challenge, with differentials including benign fibroinflammatory conditions and neoplastic processes. Imaging modalities cannot reliably distinguish between these differentials. The sampling-dependent nature of both cytopathology and core-biopsy histopathology introduces the potential for indeterminate or misleading results. Surgical biopsy can have high complication rates depending on the underlying condition. Here we report the case of a patient with chronic autoimmune thyroid disease who initially presented with fibroinflammatory thyroid disease and was subsequently diagnosed with B-cell lymphoma. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges associated with these conditions, the limitations of the sampling-dependent tissue assessment and the importance of re-evaluating the diagnosis when the clinical course is discordant with the initial biopsy findings.

title: Coexisting adrenal hemangioma and aldosterone-producing micronodule presented as adrenal incidentaloma.
abstract: Adrenal hemangiomas are rare benign vascular tumors, an uncommon cause of adrenal incidentalomas. We report a patient with coexisting adrenal hemangioma and aldosterone-producing micronodules within the same adrenal gland. A 67-year-old man was referred for an incidental left adrenal mass. Noncontrast computed tomography revealed a 1.6 × 1.4 cm lesion with an unenhanced attenuation value of 40 Hounsfield units. Initial hormonal evaluation was unremarkable except for an elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) of 115.6. On follow-up evaluation, the ARR decreased to 52.8, with a relatively low aldosterone concentration of 9.5 ng/dL (264 pmol/L; reference range, 2.52-39.2 ng/dL [69-1087 pmol/L]), yielding equivocal findings for primary aldosteronism. Serial imaging revealed growth to 3.4 × 2.8 cm over 3 years. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a T2-hyperintense lesion with peripheral nodular enhancement and delayed centripetal filling, suggestive of adrenal hemangioma. Owing to continued growth, laparoscopic adrenalectomy was performed. Histopathological examination confirmed cavernous hemangioma. Given the marked postoperative reduction in ARR to 9.7, additional pathological review identified an adjacent CYP11B2-positive aldosterone-producing micronodule. This report illustrates that adrenal incidentalomas may have dual pathologies. An integrated assessment of imaging, biochemical findings, clinical course, and histopathology, together with close clinicopathological collaboration, is essential for accurate diagnosis and management.

Given the marked postoperative reduction in ARR to 9.7, additional pathological review identified an adjacent CYP11B2-positive aldosterone-producing micronodule. This report illustrates that adrenal incidentalomas may have dual pathologies. An integrated assessment of imaging, biochemical findings, clinical course, and histopathology, together with close clinicopathological collaboration, is essential for accurate diagnosis and management.

title: Long-term cyclic ectopic adrenocorticotropic hormone syndrome with extreme fluctuations and adrenal insufficiency.
abstract: A 77-year-old woman presented with worsening glycemic control and hypokalemia and was found to have adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)-dependent hypercortisolism with loss of diurnal cortisol variation and failure of suppression on low- and high-dose dexamethasone suppression tests. Computed tomography (CT) demonstrated bilateral adrenal enlargement, whereas pituitary magnetic resonance imaging and chest CT failed to identify a source of ACTH secretion, leading to a diagnosis of occult ectopic ACTH syndrome. During 15 years of follow-up, she exhibited cyclic fluctuations in ACTH and cortisol concentrations, including episodes of severe hypercortisolism with ACTH levels exceeding 2000 pg/mL (>440 pmol/L) (reference range, 7.2-63.6 pg/mL [1.6-14.0 pmol/L]) and cortisol concentrations of 30-60 μg/dL (828-1656 nmol/L) (reference range, 6.2-19.4 μg/dL [171-535 nmol/L]), alternating with spontaneous remission. Serial imaging revealed dynamic adrenal morphological changes, with enlargement during hypercortisolemic phases and regression during remission. During treatment with ketoconazole, mitotane, and osilodrostat, the patient experienced recurrent significant hypocortisolic episodes, some of which were likely treatment-associated and required hydrocortisone replacement therapy. This case highlights an exceptionally prolonged course of cyclic ectopic ACTH syndrome characterized by extreme hormonal oscillation, reversible adrenal hyperplasia, and recurrent hypocortisolism, emphasizing the importance of long-term biochemical surveillance and individualized therapeutic adjustment.

title: When anorexia nervosa conceals Cushing syndrome: a diagnostic pitfall in hypercortisolemia.
abstract: A 37-year-old woman presented with severe hypertension, mood changes, and weight loss (body mass index 14.6 kg/m 2 ). She exhibited restrictive eating behaviors consistent with anorexia nervosa, alongside biochemical hypercortisolemia with serum cortisol 43.6 µg/dL (1204 nmol/L; reference range: 6.2-18.1 µg/dL; 170-500 nmol/L), 24-hour urinary free cortisol 430.3 µg/24 hours (1187 nmol/24 hours; reference range: <60.2 µg/24 hours; <166 nmol/24 hours), and unsuppressed adrenocorticotropic hormone of 19.1 pg/mL (4.2 pmol/L; reference range: 7.3-63.1 pg/mL; 1.6-13.9 pmol/L). The cortisol level after the 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test was 23.9 µg/dL (659 nmol/L; reference range: <1.8 µg/dL; <50 nmol/L). Cortisol remained markedly elevated after nasogastric feeding and weight restoration. Pituitary magnetic resonance imaging revealed a 4 mm left anterior pituitary lesion. High-dose dexamethasone suppression, corticotropin-releasing hormone stimulation, and inferior petrosal sinus sampling confirmed a pituitary source of adrenocorticotropic hormone. The patient underwent transsphenoidal resection of a corticotroph adenoma. Eleven months later, her hypertension and restrictive eating behaviors had resolved, and her mood significantly improved. Cushing syndrome can coexist with anorexia nervosa, masking typical cushingoid features and presenting with psychiatric manifestations and weight loss. Persistent hypercortisolemia despite nutritional rehabilitation should prompt dynamic endocrine testing and pituitary evaluation to ensure timely diagnosis and treatment.

title: Calcimimetic therapy modified the radiological, surgical, and histopathological features of a parathyroid adenoma.
abstract: Calcimimetics are increasingly used to control hypercalcemia before parathyroidectomy. Although treatment-induced degenerative changes have been reported in parathyroid adenomas, their effects on preoperative imaging and surgical planning remain unclear. A 70-year-old woman with primary hyperparathyroidism was administered preoperative evocalcet (2 mg/day). After ∼2 months, serum calcium levels decreased to the hypocalcemic range, prompting drug discontinuation before surgery referral. Upon presentation, corrected serum calcium normalized to 9.1 mg/dL (SI: 2.28 mmol/L; reference range, 8.8-10.1 mg/dL [SI: 2.20-2.53 mmol/L]), whereas intact parathyroid hormone remained mildly elevated at 65.7 pg/mL (SI: 7.0 pmol/L; reference range, 10-65 pg/mL [SI: 1.1-6.9 pmol/L]). Ultrasonography revealed a right superior parathyroid lesion, with markedly decreased Doppler flow. Four-dimensional computed tomography revealed weak enhancement throughout the contrast-enhanced phase. Parathyroidectomy revealed marked fibrosis and dense adhesions around the recurrent laryngeal nerve, making dissection technically demanding, although the nerve was preserved. Histopathological examination confirmed parathyroid adenoma with extensive fibrosis, cystic degeneration, necrosis, and macrophage infiltration. Therefore, calcimimetic therapy may modify the radiological and histopathological characteristics of parathyroid adenomas and intraoperative findings relevant to surgical planning. Recognition of these treatment-induced changes may improve the interpretation of preoperative images, help surgeons anticipate dense adhesions, and facilitate meticulous surgical dissection.

title: Primary adrenal small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma in a patient with sarcoidosis and synchronous colon adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Primary adrenal neuroendocrine carcinoma (NEC), particularly the small cell subtype, is exceptionally rare. In patients with sarcoidosis, inflammatory lymphadenopathy may mimic a metastatic disease, making disease detection difficult. A 76-year-old man with sarcoidosis was referred for an enlarging left adrenal incidentaloma that had increased in size from 7 mm to 19 × 14 mm over 3 years. Hormonal evaluation revealed unremarkable findings; laparoscopic adrenalectomy was performed because malignancy could not be excluded. Histopathological examination revealed small cell NEC with positive synaptophysin and chromogranin A staining, and a Ki-67 labeling index of 80%. One month after surgery, para-aortic lymphadenopathy was detected. Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (CT) showed uptake in the para-aortic lymph nodes and ascending colon, where colonoscopy identified synchronous adenocarcinoma. The cause of the lymphadenopathy was uncertain because of coexisting sarcoidosis and colon cancer. Cisplatin plus irinotecan induced a partial response; however, disease progression was observed. CT-guided lymph node biopsy confirmed metastatic NEC. Second-line amrubicin therapy reduced tumor size; comprehensive genomic profiling revealed a tumor mutation-burden-high phenotype. This case highlights diagnostic challenges in the evaluation of lymphadenopathy in patients with sarcoidosis and synchronous malignancy, emphasizing the importance of pathological confirmation for guiding appropriate management.

title: Diagnostic challenges of masked arginine vasopressin deficiency in neurosarcoidosis complicated by sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor use.
abstract: A wide variety of endocrine disorders caused by sarcoidosis have been reported to date. We report the case of an 82-year-old male patient who presented with hypercalcemia and anterior pituitary hormone deficiency at the time of his sarcoidosis diagnosis and was subsequently diagnosed with arginine vasopressin deficiency (AVP-D) 6 months after the initiation of glucocorticoid therapy. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed an enlarged pituitary gland, thickened pituitary stalk, and loss of the posterior pituitary bright spot, raising the suspicion of hypothalamic-pituitary sarcoidosis. Despite improvement in hypercalcemia, anterior pituitary function, and pituitary enlargement and stalk thickening with glucocorticoid therapy, subjective symptoms of dry mouth and polyuria gradually became apparent several months after the start of treatment. While the characteristic hypotonic polyuria of AVP-D was not prominent, we surmised that these typical clinical features were masked by adrenal insufficiency, chronic kidney disease (CKD), and concurrent use of a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor for type 2 diabetes. This case highlights the fact that the typical presentation of AVP-D can be masked by concurrent SGLT2 inhibitor use and CKD, emphasizing careful assessment of water balance in such patients.

title: Late-onset hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction in a childhood cancer survivor treated with cranial irradiation.
abstract: Hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction is a well-recognized late complication in childhood cancer survivors (CCSs) treated with cranial irradiation. We report a 42-year-old male with a history of acute lymphoblastic leukemia diagnosed at 5 years of age and treated with chemotherapy and 26 Gray whole-brain irradiation. He presented with right upper extremity paresis due to bilateral chronic subdural hematomas. Following burr-hole drainage for the left chronic subdural hematoma, he developed anorexia, fatigue, and hyponatremia and was referred to the endocrinology department. Endocrine evaluation demonstrated hypothalamic adrenal insufficiency, severe adult growth hormone deficiency, mild gonadal dysfunction, and mixed hypothyroidism. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a suprasellar arachnoid cyst with compression of the pituitary gland. To our knowledge, this represents one of the longest reported intervals between childhood cancer treatment and the diagnosis of hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction, which became clinically apparent 37 years after treatment following a prolonged asymptomatic period. This case suggests that hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction may remain clinically silent and gradually progress for decades before becoming unmasked by the physiological stress, highlighting the need for prolonged, potentially lifelong, endocrine surveillance in CCS.

title: Inflammatory and Autoimmune Axonal Neuropathies.
abstract: Objective This article outlines the clinical patterns, diagnostic strategies, and treatment principles for patients with inflammatory and autoimmune axonal neuropathies. Latest developments Recent studies highlight the role of serum neurofilament light chain as a biomarker of the rate of active axonal injury and the increasing use of rituximab over cyclophosphamide for induction in neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis. Imaging modalities, such as magnetic resonance neurography and fludeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET), aid in identifying biopsy targets and monitoring disease activity. Essential points Inflammatory axonal neuropathies encompass a spectrum of immune-mediated disorders presenting with mononeuritis multiplex, asymmetric sensorimotor polyneuropathy, sensory ataxia, or plexopathy. The diagnosis requires a high degree of clinical suspicion, detailed electrodiagnostic evaluation, and consideration of systemic features. Nerve biopsy, although limited by patchy yield, can confirm the diagnosis and guide immunotherapy decisions. Treatment focuses on halting inflammation and preventing relapses, with corticosteroids as first-line induction and steroid-sparing agents for maintenance. A structured follow-up approach, including standardized neurologic examinations, functional assessments, and ancillary testing, is essential for tracking disease progression and treatment response.

title: Video Head Impulse Testing for Acute Dizziness in Stroke Protocols: A Prospective Pilot Study.
abstract: Background and objectives Dizziness is a common emergency department (ED) concern, yet posterior-circulation strokes can be difficult to detect with standard clinical tools and neuroimaging alone. Quantitative video head impulse test (vHIT) provides an objective bedside measure of vestibulo-ocular reflex function and can help differentiate central from peripheral causes of acute dizziness. Methods We conducted a prospective, single-center feasibility and diagnostic-accuracy study of adults (18-90 years) presenting on an ED stroke pathway for acute dizziness. vHIT was performed within 48 hours of presentation, after completion of standard stroke evaluation. Two vestibular-trained clinicians, blinded to clinical and imaging data, classified vHIT as peripheral, central, equivocal, or poor quality. The reference standard (stroke vs nonstroke) was the final diagnosis adjudicated by stroke neurologists using all clinical information, noncontrast CT, and MRI when available. Diagnostic metrics for stroke were calculated for interpretable vHIT studies and in an intention-to-diagnose analysis. Results Thirty patients underwent vHIT; 11 (36.7%) had acute ischemic stroke and 19 (63.3%) had nonstroke diagnoses. Interpretable vHIT results (central or peripheral pattern) were obtained in 23 of 30 patients (76.7%). Overall, vHIT patterns were central in 19 (63.3%), peripheral in 4 (13.3%), equivocal in 3 (10.0%), and poor quality in 4 (13.3%). Among strokes, 9 of 11 (81.8%) had a central pattern and none had a peripheral pattern. In the primary analysis of interpretable studies, vHIT sensitivity and negative predictive value for stroke were both 100%, while specificity was 28.6% and overall accuracy was 56.5%. In the intention-to-diagnose analysis including all patients, sensitivity and negative predictive value remained 100%, with specificity at 21.1% and accuracy at 50.0%. Discussion Our findings suggest that vHIT was feasible in most ED stroke-pathway patients with acute dizziness and demonstrated high sensitivity and negative predictive value when a clearly peripheral pattern was present, supporting its potential role as an adjunctive rule-out tool. However, specificity was low, and nearly one-quarter of studies were equivocal or poor quality, limiting its use as a standalone diagnostic test. With further validation and larger studies, vHIT may help support more targeted use of hospital admissions, diagnostic workups, and ED stroke resources in patients without evidence of central pathology.

title: A Multidisciplinary Neuro-Lupus Program for the Evaluation and Management of Patients With SLE and Cognitive Concerns.
abstract: To develop and implement a standardized, comprehensive multidisciplinary program for the evaluation and management of patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and cognitive concerns that would lead to improved diagnosis and management. The Neuro-Lupus Program evaluated 50 patients with SLE referred for any neurocognitive concern over a 12-month period. A specific sequential work-up protocol was developed for standardized patient evaluation. Initial history and examination were performed by a dedicated lupus neurologist followed by referral for comprehensive neurocognitive testing. Patients with suspected mood or psychotic disorders were evaluated in a specialized autoimmune psychiatry clinic. MRI brain scans were performed in all patients. Patients with MRI evidence of inflammation or cognitive impairment were further assessed with CSF studies and FDG-PET/CT brain. Management of neuropsychiatric medications and immunotherapy was a collaboration between neurology, psychiatry, and rheumatology. Full neurocognitive evaluation revealed a previously undiagnosed cognitive impairment in 46.4% of patients tested (mild 39.3%, major 7.1%), with an additional 39.3% demonstrating a normal cognitive profile with isolated weakness. MRI demonstrated white matter disease in 50% of patients and cerebral atrophy in 10%. Brain FDG-PET/CT was performed in 8 patients (16%), 7 (88%) of which were abnormal. CSF studies demonstrated normal protein and white cell counts, but 25% had elevated kappa free light chains. As a result of this program, neuropsychiatric medications were optimized in 86% of patients and 8% had an escalation in immunotherapy. This multidisciplinary Neuro-Lupus Program model brings together neurologists, psychiatrists, rheumatologists, and neuropsychologists to standardize the approach to neurocognitive symptoms in SLE. Among the patients enrolled, this program detected previously undiagnosed cognitive impairment in the majority of those tested and was associated with changes in neuropsychiatric and immunotherapy management.

title: Functional and Structural Imaging Features of Cognitive Profiles in Multiple Sclerosis.
abstract: Background and objectives Cognitive impairment affects 40%-70% of patients with multiple sclerosis (MS). Although recent hypothesis-driven and data-driven efforts have identified cognitive phenotypes, functional substrates underlying impairment in such phenotypes are still not clear. Our objective was to identify distinct cognitive phenotypes using clustering in a large cohort of patients with MS and characterize their associated clinical, structural MRI, and resting-state (RS) functional connectivity (FC) features. Methods We conducted an observational, cross-sectional study with right-handed patients with MS and age-matched and sex-matched healthy controls (HCs) who underwent neurologic and neuropsychological evaluation (Brief Repeatable Battery of Neuropsychological tests). Latent profile analysis on cognitive test Z-scores identified MS cognitive phenotypes. 3.0T MRI was used to derive atrophy measures and RS FC within default mode network (DMN I/II), executive control network (ECN), left/right fronto-parietal, language, and salience networks. Linear regression models compared structural MRI and RS FC across cognitive phenotypes and HCs, while polynomial contrasts assessed RS FC patterns across groups. Results Three hundred and sixty-nine patients with MS and 168 HCs were enrolled. Four cognitive phenotypes were detected: preserved cognition ([PC], n = 67[18.2%]), mild single-domain verbal fluency involvement (MSD-VF, n = 37[10.0%]), mild single-domain attention involvement (MSD-A, n = 197[53.4%]), and severe multidomain (SMD) involvement (SMD, n = 68[18.4%]). At corrected threshold, PC patients showed decreased deep gray matter (GM) volumes ( p < 0.001-0.001) and similar RS FC vs HCs, whereas MSD-VF exhibited no significant atrophy and no differences in RS FC vs HCs. MSD-A displayed lower cortical/deep GM volumes vs HCs ( p < 0.001-0.005), whereas SMD had worse clinical and atrophy features ( p < 0.001-0.04), as well as decreased DMN II RS FC ( p = 0.01-0.04) vs other groups. Polynomial contrast analyses revealed significant quadratic patterns with increased RS FC in MSD-VF vs HC/PC groups, followed by decrease in MSD-A and SMD, within DMN II ( p = 0.005), ECN ( p = 0.005), and language network ( p < 0.001). Discussion PC exhibited intact RS FC, whereas SMD presented widespread structural and DMN RS FC damage. These findings advance our understanding of cognitive heterogeneity in MS by revealing distinct structural and functional neuroimaging profiles across cognitive phenotypes, encouraging future longitudinal and multimodal investigations to improve disease characterization and prognostic stratification.

Linear regression models compared structural MRI and RS FC across cognitive phenotypes and HCs, while polynomial contrasts assessed RS FC patterns across groups.

Results

Three hundred and sixty-nine patients with MS and 168 HCs were enrolled. Four cognitive phenotypes were detected: preserved cognition ([PC], n = 67[18.2%]), mild single-domain verbal fluency involvement (MSD-VF, n = 37[10.0%]), mild single-domain attention involvement (MSD-A, n = 197[53.4%]), and severe multidomain (SMD) involvement (SMD, n = 68[18.4%]). At corrected threshold, PC patients showed decreased deep gray matter (GM) volumes (p < 0.001-0.001) and similar RS FC vs HCs, whereas MSD-VF exhibited no significant atrophy and no differences in RS FC vs HCs. MSD-A displayed lower cortical/deep GM volumes vs HCs (p < 0.001-0.005), whereas SMD had worse clinical and atrophy features (p < 0.001-0.04), as well as decreased DMN II RS FC (p = 0.01-0.04) vs other groups. Polynomial contrast analyses revealed significant quadratic patterns with increased RS FC in MSD-VF vs HC/PC groups, followed by decrease in MSD-A and SMD, within DMN II (p = 0.005), ECN (p = 0.005), and language network (p < 0.001).

Discussion

PC exhibited intact RS FC, whereas SMD presented widespread structural and DMN RS FC damage. These findings advance our understanding of cognitive heterogeneity in MS by revealing distinct structural and functional neuroimaging profiles across cognitive phenotypes, encouraging future longitudinal and multimodal investigations to improve disease characterization and prognostic stratification.

title: Portable Ultra-Low-Field MRI in Neurologic Diseases: Current Status and Potential in Clinical Practice, Research, and Trials.
abstract: Neurologic diseases are highly prevalent, and MRI plays a crucial role in their diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment monitoring. Conventional MRI at high magnetic field strength (≥1.5 tesla) is one of the most widely used modalities in clinical practice and a common outcome measure in clinical trials. Despite its importance and effectiveness, challenges, such as high cost, limited accessibility, and disease-related constraints, can hinder its widespread use. Recent advancements in portable ultra-low-field (<0.1 tesla) MRI technology offer potential solutions by enabling point-of-care brain imaging for neurologic diseases. However, the substantially lower magnetic field strength results in lower signal-to-noise ratio, reduced spatial resolution, and more limited imaging contrast, although ongoing computational approaches aim to mitigate some of these limitations. In this narrative review, we examine current evidence on applications of portable ultra-low-field MRI to neurologic disorders, discussing the technology's utility, limitations, and clinical implications. In addition, we highlight key open research questions and future opportunities for further integration of this emerging technology.

title: Spinal Cord and Nerve Root Involvement in Histiocytic Neoplasms: A Retrospective Observational Cohort Study.
abstract: Background and objectives Histiocytic neoplasms, including Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD), Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH), and Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes disease (RDD), have frequent nervous system involvement. The aim of this study was to characterize the neurologic, radiologic, and laboratory features of spinal cord and nerve root involvement in histiocytic neoplasms. Methods We evaluated patients with biopsy-proven ECD, LCH, or RDD seen at a tertiary referral center between January 1996 and December 2024. Patients were included if spinal MRI demonstrated spinal cord or nerve root involvement. Spinal MRI was performed for evaluation of myelopathic or radicular symptoms or as part of staging in patients with CNS involvement. We collected demographic variables, neurologic syndromes and imaging patterns, treatment characteristics, and outcomes including disability (Expanded Disability Status Scale [EDSS] score) and ambulatory status. The primary outcome was neurologic disability at nadir and last follow-up; secondary outcomes included radiographic patterns and clinical response to treatment. Data were summarized descriptively, with exploratory group comparisons performed using parametric or nonparametric tests as appropriate. Results Among 415 patients with ECD (n = 183), LCH (n = 144), or RDD (n = 88), spinal cord or nerve root involvement was identified in 42 (ECD, 27; LCH, 4; RDD, 11). The median age at onset was 43.1 years (interquartile range 32.1-58.5), and 18 (43%) were female. Most cases were symptomatic (36/42, 86%), with myelopathy as the first neurologic manifestation in 26 (72%). Parenchymal infiltration predominated in the ECD group (17/27, 63%), compared with LCH (2/4, 50%) and RDD (2/11, 18%) groups (Fisher exact test across groups, p = 0.035). Root involvement was more frequent in the RDD group (8/11, 73%) than in the ECD (7/27, 26%) or LCH (1/4, 25%) group (Fisher exact test across groups, p = 0.021). The median EDSS score at nadir was 4.0; 43% required ambulatory aid or worse. After treatment, 22 of 36 symptomatic patients (61%) improved clinically and radiographically, more often in RDD (10/11, 91%) and LCH (2/3, 67%) groups than in the ECD group (10/22, 46%; Fisher exact test across groups, p = 0.022). At a median 5.8-year follow-up, 8 of 38 survivors (21%) required ambulatory assistance or were nonambulatory. Discussion Spinal cord and nerve root involvement occurs in histiocytic neoplasms. These findings support prioritizing spinal MRI in patients with neurologic symptoms or high-risk disease features because early identification may inform diagnosis and management.

title: Association Between Plasma N-Terminal Tau, Cognitive Decline, and Neurodegeneration in the ADNI Cohort.
abstract: Background and objectives Blood-based biomarkers offer a cost-effective, minimally invasive alternative to neuroimaging and CSF biomarkers. Newly developed fluid biomarkers, including the N-terminal tau fragment (NT1), show promise for identifying individuals at risk for Alzheimer disease (AD) and for monitoring disease progression. Here, we determine whether NT1 levels are associated with key clinical and biomarker measures in a large, well-characterized cohort. Methods Participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort with available plasma NT1, β-amyloid (Aβ)-PET, MRI, and clinical measures (Clinical Dementia Rating) were included in this observational study. NT1 was measured using the Quanterix Simoa HD-X platform. PET, MRI, clinical, and other plasma measures were obtained using established ADNI procedures. A subset also had NULISA-based plasma measures of amyloid and tau and tau-PET assessed. Linear regression and linear mixed-effects models were used to assess cross-sectional and longitudinal associations between NT1 and clinical or biomarker measures, adjusting for relevant covariates. Multivariable-adjusted Cox regression was performed to evaluate the association between baseline NT1 levels and risk of clinically diagnosed mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or AD. Mediation analysis was conducted to examine whether hippocampal atrophy mediates the relationship between NT1 and memory decline. Spearman correlations were used to examine continuous relationships between plasma NT1 and continuous fluid and neuroimaging markers. Results A total of 755 participants (mean age: 72.9 [7.0], female: 375 [50%]) were included in the study. Plasma NT1 levels were elevated in MCI/AD individuals (B MCI/AD [SE] = 0.09 [0.022], p = 1.98 × 10 -4 ) and were cross-sectionally associated with worse memory performance (B [SE] = -0.25 [0.09], p = 0.005). Aβ moderated the association between elevated NT1 and greater cognitive decline across multiple domains (memory: B [SE] = -0.17 [0.074], p = 0.022; executive function: B [SE] = -0.24 [0.082], p = 0.004; language: B [SE] = -0.21 [0.075], p = 0.006). NT1 levels were negatively associated with hippocampal volume (B [SE] = -264.49 [125.99], p = 0.036) and predicted longitudinal atrophy (B [SE] = -42.00 [16.90], p = 0.013). Accelerated hippocampal atrophy largely mediated the association between higher baseline NT1 level and greater memory decline (B [95% CI] indirect effect = -0.082 [-0.135 to -0.03], p = 0.003, B [95% CI] proportion mediated = 70.1% [32.6%-155.3%], p = 0.004). Higher NT1 levels were associated with higher levels of plasma biomarkers, including NULISA-based brain-derived (BD) plasma pTau (BD-pTau181, BD-pTau217, BD-pTau231: p 's < 5.01 × 10 -6 ) and Simoa-Based pTau181 ( p < 4.51 × 10 -15 ) and neurofilament light chain ( p < 5.34 × 10 -7 ). Discussion Plasma NT1 may be useful in assessing amyloid-dependent cognitive decline and neurodegeneration.

title: Pearls & Oy-sters: Diagnosis of Pediatric Tumefactive Multiple Sclerosis With MRI Biomarkers.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a demyelinating disease of the CNS with an estimated incidence of 0.05-2.85 per 100,000 children. One subtype, tumefactive MS, is particularly rare and difficult to diagnose, especially in differentiating from tumor. We describe the case of a 16-year-old boy who presented with subacute onset of headaches, cognitive difficulties, dizziness, blurry vision, right arm weakness, numbness, and gait difficulty. MRI of the brain demonstrated a multilobulated, contrast-enhancing, T2 hyperintense area of diffusion restriction in the left frontal lobe, an extensive left periventricular lesion, and multifocal T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintense lesions. He clinically improved with IV steroids and a 1-month oral steroid taper, and then, 2 weeks after completion of the taper, he experienced recurrent headaches and cognitive decline. Repeat brain MRI (3T) with MS protocol which included 3D T2* gradient recalled echo was notable for lesions demonstrating central vein sign (CVS) and paramagnetic rim-like areas within the large left frontal lesion characterized by positive phase shift and associated contrast enhancement. Based on the presence of typical symptoms, multiple enhancing and nonenhancing lesions in the periventricular and juxtacortical regions, and 6 CVS-positive lesions, the patient met 2024 McDonald criteria, and the diagnosis of MS was made. The patient was treated with IV steroids followed by oral steroids and then started on ocrelizumab. This case demonstrates how recognition of CVS is critical, because early and accurate diagnosis enables timely treatment without unnecessary interventions.

title: Association of Skin Denervation With Brain Atrophy and Cognitive Impairment in Patients With Parkinson Disease.
abstract: Background and objectives Small fiber pathology is an intrinsic feature of Parkinson disease (PD), yet its relevance to central neurodegeneration remains unclear. Given that cognitive impairment is a major manifestation of disease progression closely linked to cortical structural changes, we aimed to determine whether peripheral skin denervation is associated with cognitive impairment and brain atrophy in PD. Methods In this cross-sectional study at a movement disorders center in China, patients with PD and healthy controls (HCs) were recruited. Key inclusion criteria included a clinical PD diagnosis based on the Movement Disorder Society criteria and an age range of 50-99 years. Patients were classified into normal cognition (PD-NC), mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI), and patients develop dementia (PDD). All participants underwent skin biopsy for quantification of intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD), neuropsychological assessments, and structural MRI. Multivariable regression and mediation analyses examined associations among IENFD, cognition, and brain volumes. Results A total of 155 patients with PD (mean age, 63.4 years; 52% female; PD-NC: n = 75; PD-MCI: n = 40; PDD: n = 40) and 50 HCs (mean age, 60.3 years; 50% female) were included. IENFD demonstrated a progressive decline across the PD cognitive spectrum (HC: 7.18 ± 2.44; PD-NC: 5.89 ± 2.05; PD-MCI: 4.65 ± 1.33; PDD: 3.40 ± 1.15 fibers/mm). IENFD positively correlated with global and 5 domain-specific cognitive scores (β = 0.170-0.387, p < 0.05). Lower IENFD was independently associated with an increased risk of cognitive impairment (odds ratio = 0.541, 95% CI 0.420-0.697) and showed good diagnostic performance in distinguishing PD-MCI and PDD from PD-NC (area under the ROC curve = 0.772, 95% CI 0.697-0.838). Furthermore, IENFD correlated with frontal and insular gray matter volumes (β = 0.155-0.195, p < 0.05), which statistically mediated the associations between IENFD and cognitive performance (proportion mediated for global cognition: 8.0%-10.2%). Discussion Our study suggests that skin denervation is closely associated with cognitive impairment in PD and that regional brain atrophy statistically mediates this relationship. These findings provide novel evidence for the peripheral-central axis in PD, suggesting that small fiber pathology may mirror central neurodegeneration. Future multicenter and longitudinal studies are required for validation.

title: Clinical Factors Associated With Discordant Plasma P-Tau217 and Established Alzheimer Disease Biomarkers.
abstract: Background and objectives Plasma phosphorylated tau (p-tau) 217 is increasingly used for Alzheimer disease (AD) diagnosis and treatment decisions but may be discordant with established AD biomarkers. False-positive (FP) plasma results may lead to overtreatment and false-negative (FN) results to missed or delayed disease-modifying therapies. We evaluated factors associated with discordant results. Methods This retrospective study included participants enrolled in memory and aging studies at Mayo Clinic with "positive" (>0.324 pg/mL) or "negative" (<0.186 pg/mL) plasma p-tau217 results and confirmatory AD biomarkers. Plasma results were classified as true positive (TP), true negative (TN), FP, or FN, referencing amyloid-PET and CSF p-tau181/β-amyloid (Aβ) 42. Clinical and laboratory variables were compared using univariate analyses; multivariable logistic regression evaluated independent associations with discordance. Results Among 706 participants (median 70.0 [interquartile range 15.8] years; 54% male), 60 (8.5%) had discordant plasma p-tau217 results. FN results (5.6%) were more frequent than FP results (2.8%; p = 0.007). Discordance was associated with older age (odds ratio [OR] 1.61 per decade, 95% CI 1.23-2.14) and obstructive sleep apnea (OR 1.94, 95% CI 1.08-3.49). FN (vs TP) results were associated with milder clinical stage (global Clinical Dementia Rating [CDR] ≤0.5 vs CDR ≥1; p < 0.001), higher Mini-Mental State Examination scores (OR 1.20 per point, 95% CI 1.05-1.36), obstructive sleep apnea (OR 2.01, 95% CI 1.01-4.3), higher body mass index (OR 1.11/kg/m 2 , 95% CI 1.03-1.20), and higher estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR: OR 1.33/10 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , 95% CI 1.05-1.69). In age-adjusted models, body mass index (OR 1.14, 95% CI 1.03-1.25), eGFR (OR 1.63/10 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , 95% CI 1.22-2.16), and earlier clinical stage (CDR ≤0.5) were independently associated with FN results. FP (vs TN) results were associated with older age (OR 2.37, 95% CI 1.36-4.09), thyroid disease (OR 4.41, 95% CI 1.36-14.3), lower eGFR (OR 0.48/10 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , 95% CI 0.31-0.66), and advanced disease stage (CDR ≥1). In age-adjusted models, eGFR (OR 0.54/10 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , 95% CI 0.35-0.82) and advanced disease stage (CDR ≥ 1 vs CDR 0: OR 11.11, 95% CI 2.0-50.0; vs CDR 0.5: OR 4.55, 95% CI 1.12-16.67) were independently associated with FP results. Discussion Plasma p-tau217 results and established AD biomarkers were discordant in 8.5% of participants. Clinical stage and factors related to brain amyloid clearance, renal clearance, and volume of distribution were associated with discordant results. These insights may inform mechanisms of discordance and identify patients requiring confirmatory biomarker measures.
